title: SUVAT equations
examples: When do I know which equation to use?
Can you explain the sign convention for acceleration?
What if the object changes direction?

explain.say: Today we learn the SUVAT equations for motion.

draw.text: SUVAT equations: v, u, a, t

explain.say: The equations help us find motion details when acceleration is constant.
First we must choose the right equation based on what we know.
If you know initial velocity, final velocity, and time, use this one.
For example, a car starting from rest moves at ten meters per second.

faq.q: What does the 's' stand for in these equations?
faq.a: The letter s stands for displacement, which is the change in position.

faq.q: If the object is moving at a constant speed, what is the acceleration?
faq.a: If the speed is constant, the acceleration is zero. You can use the simplest equations then.
asks: What is 'a' if it is not speeding up?
If acceleration is zero, what happens?

faq.q: How do I handle negative numbers for velocity?
faq.a: Negative signs mean the object is moving in the opposite direction to your starting point.
asks: When should I use negative signs?
Does negative velocity mean something else?

faq.q: Can I use these equations if the acceleration is not constant?
faq.a: No, these specific equations only work when the acceleration value is constant throughout the motion.
asks: Do these work for curved paths?
What if the acceleration changes over time?

faq.q: If I am asked how far before stopping, which equation helps me?
faq.a: You can use the equation that relates final velocity, initial velocity, and displacement.
asks: How do I find distance when stopping?
What formula relates distance to stopping?

facts: Displacement is the change in position, measured in meters.
Velocity is the rate of change of displacement over time.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
If an object stops, its final velocity is zero.

quiz.say: A runner starts from rest and accelerates at two meters per second squared. What is the displacement after three seconds?
quiz.why: You use the equation s equals u t plus one half a t squared. This gives you zero plus one half times two times three squared, which is nine meters.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you calculated only u times t, forgetting the acceleration part of the formula.
wrong.1: This is wrong because you multiplied acceleration by time squared, instead of using one half times the acceleration.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you only used the time value, ignoring the effect of acceleration.

quiz.say: A ball thrown upwards has a final velocity of zero at its highest point. If it started with a velocity of fifteen meters per second, how far did it travel?
quiz.why: You use the equation v squared equals u squared plus two a s. Since gravity causes negative acceleration, you get zero equals fifteen squared plus two times negative nine times s, making s equal to seventy-two divided by negative eighteen, which is negative four meters. The distance is the positive value.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you only used the initial velocity, ignoring the effect of gravity on the distance.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the ball travels up to a certain height, even if its final velocity is zero at that peak.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you calculated u squared, forgetting to account for the change in velocity due to gravity.

quiz.say: A train brakes from a speed of thirty meters per second to a stop over a distance of one hundred meters. What was its acceleration?
quiz.why: You use the equation v squared equals u squared plus two a s. You get zero equals thirty squared plus two times a times one hundred, so a equals negative nine hundred divided by two hundred, which is negative fifteen.

wrong.0: This is wrong because you forgot to include the negative sign, which indicates deceleration.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the train is clearly slowing down, meaning there must be a non-zero acceleration.
wrong.2: This is wrong because you incorrectly rearranged the formula, squaring the initial velocity term twice.
